paragraphs: This checklist is for self-questioning only. It does not constitute hiring criteria, an ability score, or a conclusion about the quality or safety of work and services. This page follows the US O*NET-SOC 27-1023.00 occupation, Floral Designers (the fixed index assigns this asset the Chinese name for floral designers; the main work involves designing, cutting, and arranging fresh, dried, or artificial flowers and foliage into bouquets, wreaths, table arrangements, and scene decorations).

Practice prompt | A shop receives a completely fictional order for a small wedding setup (ceremony area and reception table flowers). Write a floral design proposal covering: (1) how to confirm the occasion, style, colors, budget, and delivery time and location with the customer; (2) how to select materials to suit the requirements and specify estimated proportions and quantities of focal flowers, supporting materials, and foliage; (3) how to arrange incoming flower inspection, cutting and conditioning, preservation, and temperature and humidity control; (4) how to design colors and forms and explain alternatives for different containers and settings; and (5) how to check finished work before delivery (freshness, stability, color discrepancies, and packaging) and retain reviewable records. Use public information and simulated dimensions; do not use any real customer, address, or contract information.

Fit signals | O*NET highlights: daily face-to-face discussions with individuals and teams (100%), daily telephone communication (95%), work in controlled indoor environments (91%), continuous handling and control of materials and tools with both hands (86% continually or almost continually), daily decision-making (68%), daily time pressure (86%), continuous standing (73%), repetitive motions (55%), contact with external customers being extremely important (55%), and some freedom to determine tasks and priorities (57%); the work also requires Thinking Creatively and organizing work around customer requirements. If you are willing to keep making things by hand, are sensitive to color and form, and can balance aesthetics and delivery during holiday peaks, this occupation's daily demands are closer to your working style.

Caution signals | O*NET also shows daily time pressure (86%), daily telephone communication (95%), continuous standing (73%) and hand use (86%), and repetitive motions (55%). Most floral designers work in retail flower shops and supermarket floral departments, with concentrated overtime common during holiday and wedding peaks (such as Valentine's Day, Mother's Day, Qixi, Qingming, and year-end holidays). Daily work uses sharp tools such as floral shears, knives, and wire, involves pollen and plant sap, and requires careful flower preservation and loss management (temperature and humidity, refrigeration, and payment terms). If you find prolonged standing and repetitive hand movements difficult, feel excessive pressure from flower losses and last-minute customer changes, or struggle with peak holiday schedules, treat these as practical costs to weigh carefully.

Responsibility judgment | Real fit depends on whether you can accomplish three things together at an actual shop's pace: meet delivery requirements (confirming occasion and budget, selecting materials and colors, preserving and conditioning flowers, and delivering on time), produce consistent finished work (fresh, stable, proportionate, with accurate packaging and cards), and take responsibility for reviewable records throughout ordering and delivery (quotes, losses, changes, and delivery records). Test this through a verifiable experience, such as peak-season work in a flower shop, a short floral training course with a completed piece, or an actual setup for a family or friends' event, rather than relying solely on an interest questionnaire.

Safe work sample (a completely fictional task package): Given a simulated brief for a small wedding (occasion, style, colors, budget range, and venue plan), complete a floral design proposal within 60 minutes: a requirements confirmation record (occasion, style, colors, budget, and delivery time and location), material selection and quantity estimates (proportions and quantities of focal flowers, supporting materials, and foliage), an incoming inspection and conditioning plan (arrival checks, cutting and hydration, preservation, and temperature and humidity control), a color and form plan (including container and setting alternatives), and a pre-delivery checklist (freshness, stability, color discrepancies, and packaging). Specify situations requiring a pause and escalation rather than handling them yourself, such as conflicting budget and requirements, flowers subject to quarantine restrictions or of unknown origin, or inadequate venue safety conditions.

O*NET27-1023.00 covers designing, cutting, and arranging fresh, dried, or artificial flowers and foliage. The directory includes customer reception, financial records, gift sales, payment collection, delivery, shop displays, event decoration, and mentoring; retail payment collection cannot be categorically excluded. Specialist cultivation, overall exhibition design, or structural construction can be distinguished as adjacent responsibilities. Check specialist qualifications and authority concerning venues, food (where edible products are actually involved), and quarantine by jurisdiction; an occupational directory is not a licensing list.

entries: Requirements confirmation | Occasion and budget | Confirm the occasion (everyday, holiday, wedding, funeral, or business), style and color preferences, budget range, and delivery time and location with the customer, then use these to determine the design direction.

Material selection and purchasing | Flowers and supporting materials | Select fresh, dried, or artificial flowers and foliage to suit requirements, order from wholesalers and growers, and check varieties, grades, quantities, and arrival times.

Incoming inspection and conditioning | Preservation and hydration | Check quantity and quality, remove leaves, cut and condition stems, remove damaged petals, store flowers in separate areas according to their characteristics, and control temperature and humidity.

Design and production | Color and form | Design bouquets, wreaths, table arrangements, and corsages using proportion, color, and texture, securing them with floral foam, vessels, wire, and floral tape to ensure stability.
Packaging and delivery | Pricing and transport | Complete packaging, ribbons, and cards, calculate costs and quotes, arrange or perform delivery, and finish setup and reinforcement on site.

Shop operations and after-sales service | Displays and care instructions | Maintain shop and window displays, manage stock and losses, explain care and handling to customers, and train or mentor others.

paragraphs:
Work context | O*NET 27-1023.00 work context indicates controlled indoor environments, continuous hands-on production, and intensive customer communication; specific conditions vary with shop type, peak season, and delivery setting.
Face-to-face communication | Daily face-to-face discussions with individuals and teams (100%), requiring in-person confirmation of requirements, style, and delivery details.
Telephone communication | Daily telephone communication (95%) for orders, confirmations, and delivery coordination.
Indoor environment | Daily work in controlled indoor environments (91%); some roles involve moving between refrigerated and room-temperature areas.
Time pressure | Daily time pressure (86%), with concentrated overtime during holiday and wedding peaks and fixed delivery deadlines.
Hands-on work | Continually handling, controlling, or touching materials and tools with both hands (86% continually or almost continually), and continuous standing (73%).
Repetitive motions | Repetitive motions (55% continually or almost continually), with frequent cutting, leaf stripping, and tying.
Decisions and authority | Daily decision-making (68%), with some freedom (50%); some freedom to determine tasks and priorities (57%).
Customer contact | Contact with external customers is extremely important (55%); decisions affect colleagues and shop outcomes (50% important outcomes).

Environment and pace | Most roles are in retail flower shops and supermarket floral departments, in indoor environments with controlled temperature and humidity (O*NET 91% daily), but often require carrying materials between refrigerated areas and workbenches. The pace follows holiday calendars and wedding bookings, with peaks at Valentine's Day, Mother's Day, Qixi, Qingming, and year-end holidays. Peak periods require early receipt of stock, consecutive production shifts, and nighttime deliveries; quieter periods focus on shop displays, inventory care, and everyday retail. Flowers have a short shelf life and are sensitive to losses, so quotes and quantity estimates must reflect incoming quality; misjudgment directly causes waste and customer complaints. Physical demands center on prolonged standing, repetitive hand movements, and carrying water tanks and flower buckets. Use protective equipment as required and prevent slips in refrigerated and wet areas.

Tools and materials | Equipment: floral and pruning shears, floral knives, thorn strippers, wire and floral tape, floral foam and absorbent sponges, staplers, preservatives, refrigerated cabinets, flower buckets and water tubes, wrapping paper and ribbons, card-printing tools, and checkout and order equipment. Materials: fresh, dried, and artificial flowers, various foliage and supporting materials, floral vessels and containers, preservatives, and cleaning and disinfecting supplies. Information: supplier and wholesaler catalogs, flower conditioning and preservation instructions, order and quotation records, stock and loss ledgers, and delivery and venue access requirements. All preservation and conditioning parameters (hydration time, refrigeration temperature, and preservative ratios) must follow the product and supplier instructions valid for the current shift.

Confirm requirements and budget → Select materials and place orders → Inspect arrivals, cut, and condition → Design colors and produce arrangements → Package, price, deliver, and set up → Check delivery and explain care

Editorial check: Check condition, proportions and colors, fastening, packaging and cards, and delivery against the actual fresh, dried, or artificial flowers and order requirements. Dehydration or fresh-flower preservation indicators do not apply to all artificial or dried flowers; check access and site conditions against actual requirements. Obtain the appropriate confirmation before key substitutions.

Adjacent responsibility boundaries | This page covers O*NET-SOC 27-1023.00. Adjacent but distinct occupations include Craft Artists (focused on individual craft and artistic creation, with work that can be retained long term), Fine Artists (focused on fine art creation and exhibition), Graphic Designers (focused on visual graphic design and prepress production), Merchandise Displayers and Window Trimmers (focused on merchandise displays and shop windows), Set and Exhibit Designers (focused on overall exhibition and scene design), and Retail Salespersons (focused on product sales and service). These occupations differ in objects, techniques, retention periods, and authority. Venue construction, structural safety, quarantine, and compliance judgments belong to the relevant trades and responsible parties; this occupation does not replace their judgment or sign-off.

Boundary review points | Pause and escalate when: customer requirements clearly conflict with the budget or delivery deadline; specified flowers cannot be obtained because of seasonality, quarantine, or source-compliance restrictions (inform the customer and offer alternatives; do not conceal substitutions); the venue has access, fire, or structural hazards; large installations or work at height require professional construction; religious, customary, or privacy requirements for weddings or funerals need specific confirmation; or supplier payment terms exceed the role's authority. The shop supervisor, project lead, or appropriately licensed party must handle these situations under the contract and applicable requirements.

Receive requirements → Confirm occasion, style, and budget → Select materials and order → Inspect arrivals, cut, and condition → Design and produce → Package and deliver → Check delivery and hand over care instructions

Difference from craft-artists (Craft Artists): They create craft works that can be retained long term through individual craftsmanship and artistic expression, with evaluation emphasizing artistry and technique. This occupation responds to settings and customer needs, producing mostly short-lived fresh-flower items, evaluated for freshness, timely delivery, and on-site effect. Materials, retention periods, and business models differ.

Difference from fine-artists-including-painters-sculptors-and-illustrators (Fine Artists, Including Painters, Sculptors, and Illustrators): They focus on fine art creation, exhibition, and commissioned artworks. This occupation is an applied service craft that produces deliverable fresh-flower works within limited time according to customer requirements, and does not involve the systems for long-term artwork preservation and copyright licensing.

Difference from merchandise-displayers-and-window-trimmers (Merchandise Displayers and Window Trimmers): They focus on merchandise displays and window visuals, mainly using durable goods and props. This occupation handles living or perishable floral materials, emphasizing preservation, conditioning, and timeliness. Finished pieces change over time and require replacement; material properties and maintenance needs differ.

Difference from set-and-exhibit-designers (Set and Exhibit Designers): They handle overall design, structures, and construction for exhibitions, film and television, and event settings, involving engineering and safety. This occupation focuses on floral forms and arrangements and does not undertake structural construction, electrical design, or fire-safety design. Project scale, authority, and responsibility boundaries differ.

Before choosing this occupation, compare actual tasks (the proportions of everyday retail, holiday orders, and wedding and event setups), qualification and training routes (on-the-job training, floral courses, and industry association certification), shifts and physical demands (peak-season overtime, prolonged standing, and repetitive hand movements), health costs (allergies to pollen and plant sap, tool cuts, and refrigerated environments), and progression routes (senior floral designer, shop supervisor, event floral coordinator, or independent studio). Regions and shops differ substantially; check actual vacancies, shop observations, and feedback on completed work.

Responsibility boundaries cannot be inferred from similar job titles: Even among design or arrangement roles, craft creation, fine art, graphic design, merchandise display, exhibition construction, and floral design differ in objects, materials, retention periods, delivery deadlines, and authority. Moving between fields requires learning the materials and techniques anew; judgment and sign-off authority from the original field do not carry over. Projects involving structures, electricity, and fire safety must be handled by the relevant specialists.

AI task exposure | Digital tools may assist with order and inventory records, trial quotes and quantity calculations, searches for color and form inspiration, initial drafts of shop social media and display content, and delivery scheduling reminders. However, floral designers and shop supervisors remain responsible for judging occasion and budget, flower freshness and conditioning, final color and form choices, on-site production and setup, customer communication, and delivery. Task exposure does not equal job replacement.

Adoption conditions | Digital tools used in shops and setup sites must meet these conditions: outputs are traceable and reviewable and do not replace actual on-site judgment of flowers and venues; recordkeeping and reminders do not displace actual conditioning and delivery time; and estimates for quotes, quantities, and schedules must be confirmed by the shop supervisor before use in ordering and settlement. A technical demonstration does not mean organizational adoption and does not change responsibilities for flower preservation, food safety (if edible decorations are involved), or venue safety.

Data and system prerequisites | Before adoption, check whether order and quotation records can be traced to original requirements; the definitions and update frequency of inventory and loss data; access permissions and retention periods for customer and event information; whether software works offline when the shop has no network connection; whether delivery and venue information uses definitions consistent with third-party systems; and whether the basis of automatically generated color and quantity suggestions can be traced.

Human control points and review | Floral designers and shop supervisors must judge occasion and budget, flower freshness and conditioning, color and form choices, on-site production and setup, delivery confirmation, and after-sales handling. Any tool-generated quotes, quantities, schedules, and content drafts must undergo human review before use, with evidence of the checks retained.

Remaining responsibilities | Matters that must not be automatically approved include whether flowers are safe to use and subject to source or quarantine restrictions, whether finished pieces meet delivery standards, confirmation of customer changes and additional charges, and setup decisions involving venue safety and compliance. No tool output constitutes a finding of acceptability or an authorization decision.

Failure risks | Unreviewed tool outputs may directly cause incorrect quotes and quantity estimates, distorted inventory and loss records, delivery schedule conflicts, or on-site execution of unconfirmed colors and substitutions as though already agreed, resulting in flower waste, delayed delivery, and customer complaints. Before implementation, specify who reviews outputs and which original information they use.

Employment evidence boundaries | Employment and wage data for this occupation must distinguish statistical scopes: US figures from O*NET and BLS are estimates under specific definitions and cannot be directly extrapolated to mainland China or other regions. China uses industry average wages as background proxies, which do not establish occupational wages. All generated content should be traceable to original inputs and sources; fluent wording is not evidence of correctness.

Practical response | First use digital tools in reversible, auditable, low-risk steps, such as organizing orders, recording inventory and losses, trial quotation calculations, and delivery reminders, subject to shop supervisor confirmation and actual delivery outcomes. Decide whether to expand use based on error records and customer feedback; aesthetic and delivery judgments must always retain human confirmation.

Cross-market statistical boundaries | Mainland China and the United States use different industry and occupational classification systems. Mainland China publishes average wages for employees in urban units by national economic industry category, without separate figures for this occupation; the United States provides estimates by SOC occupation and industry. The two cannot be combined or converted, and industry averages cannot replace occupational wages.

Insufficient evidence: Mainland China has no established public occupational wage statistic precisely matching floral designers; industry averages, advertised pay, and third-party estimates are not used to fill the gap.

Mainland China wage evidence review points | This page provides only statistical definitions, industry background proxies, and visible evidence-gap records, without estimated pay for this occupation. Before using any figure, confirm whether its statistical scope (industry category / occupation), period, unit, and covered population are comparable with this occupation.

US wage evidence review points | US figures on this page come from BLS OEWS May 2025 and BLS 2025—2035 employment projections. Before use, confirm the occupational scope (SOC 27-1023), whether overtime and benefits are included (OEWS excludes them), and whether the figures are national rather than specific to a region or employer.

Mainland China wage evidence—market scope | The National Bureau of Statistics publishes average wages for employees in urban units by industry category, covering urban units nationwide without an occupational breakdown. Average wages in relevant categories such as wholesale and retail trade provide background reference only and cannot replace occupational wages. Employment arrangements vary substantially among flower shops, supermarket floral departments, wedding and event companies, and independent studios, making them difficult for public statistics to cover.
Insufficient evidence: No median wage for floral designers verifiable by occupation has been obtained for mainland China; industry-category averages are not used to fill the gap.

Mainland China wage evidence—statistical period | Industry average wages are annual figures (the figures below are for 2025, published in 2026), unlike the US May 2025 wage reference point on this page. The two periods must not be mixed.

Cross-market statistical boundaries | Mainland China industry average wages and US occupational wages differ in statistical subjects, periods, and definitions. This page presents them separately with limitations, without exchange-rate conversion or treating industry averages as occupational wages.

Mainland China wage evidence—units | The National Bureau of Statistics reports annual average wages in yuan / year, using total pre-tax wages (including individual income tax and employee social insurance and housing provident fund contributions withheld by the employer). US OEWS reports dollars / hour or dollars / year, excluding overtime, bonuses, and benefits. Units and included components differ and cannot be directly compared.

Insufficient evidence: No wage data for floral designers verifiable by region or employment arrangement has been obtained for mainland China; individual quotes and secondhand accounts are not used to fill the gap.

Mainland China wage evidence—covered population | Urban non-private unit statistics cover employees of non-private legal entities in urban areas, while urban private unit statistics cover private-unit employees. Neither covers individually owned businesses, freelancers, or casual employment. Individual businesses, per-order pay, and part-time peak-season work common in flower shops and weddings differ substantially and are difficult for public statistics to cover.

US wage evidence—market scope | BLS OEWS provides sample-survey estimates representing employer-reported wages, excluding self-employment and the commission portion of income. The median is the distribution midpoint, not starting pay or the level at any particular region or employer.

US wage evidence—statistical period | Wages are from May 2025 OEWS; employment, growth, and openings are from 2025—2035 employment projections. The two types of data have different reference points and must not be combined as conclusions for a single point in time.

US wage evidence—units | Figures are published in dollars / hour and dollars / year. Annual mean wages are converted to a full-year, full-time basis; converting hourly and annual figures does not establish an individual's actual income, which also depends on hours, peak-season overtime, and seasonality.

US wage evidence—covered population | Covers employees reported by nonfarm establishment employers, excluding self-employment, family operations, and unreported cash-paid work. Independent orders and peak-season casual work common in flower shops and event floristry are difficult to cover fully.

US wage evidence—occupational scope | Figures on this page correspond to SOC 27-1023 (Floral Designers), excluding fine art creation (27-1013), craft artists (27-1012), graphic design (27-1024), merchandise display and window trimming (27-1026), and exhibition design (27-1024 series). Wages across occupations must not be mixed.

US wage evidence—sampling and missing-data limitations | OEWS provides sample estimates subject to sampling error; breakdowns by industry and region may have missing or unreliable estimates. This occupation has a moderate employment size (about 45,200 in 2025, the BLS employment-projection base year; OEWS May 2025 shows about 40,590), making detailed industry estimates more prone to gaps. This page has not obtained industry-specific wages readable by industry and records this as a visible gap; industry averages and third-party estimates are not substituted.

paragraphs: Conclusion | The core differences between this occupation and adjacent occupations concern what they work with, what they deliver, and how long it lasts. This occupation works with fresh, dried, and artificial flowers and foliage, delivering fresh-flower pieces that change over time within customer deadlines. Craft artists and fine artists focus on individual creation and retaining works; graphic designers deliver visual designs and prepress files; merchandise displayers and window trimmers mainly display durable goods and props; set and exhibit designers handle overall exhibition and scene design and construction; retail salespersons focus on product sales and service. Material properties, delivery deadlines, authority, and responsibility boundaries differ; judgment and sign-off authority cannot be carried across fields.

Evidence note | Comparisons in the table below come from O*NET occupational classifications and publicly available sales information. They help distinguish adjacent occupations' work and suitability of choice; they do not establish qualifications, hiring, or pay. Wages and employment for each occupation must be checked separately under its own SOC scope. This table does not compare figures or use one occupation's wages as a proxy for another.

Introduction | The comparison uses four columns: occupational direction, core work and outputs, key differences, and choices it better suits. Adjacent occupations collaborate (for example, floral designers provide wedding flowers while exhibition and construction teams handle structures and lighting), but collaboration does not make them interchangeable. Choosing another field requires learning its materials, techniques, requirements, and acceptance standards anew.

Centers on selecting, combining, preserving, and shaping floral materials. Judgments of freshness and conditioning, colors and proportions, timely delivery, and on-site effect determine finished quality; pieces change over time.

Better suited to people sensitive to color and form who want ongoing hands-on production and direct customer contact; those able to accept intense holiday peaks and flower-loss management pressure are a closer fit.

Outputs are floral pieces and setups: requirements confirmation, material selection and ordering, incoming inspection and conditioning, design and production, packaging and pricing, delivery and setup, and care instructions.
This occupation: Floral Designers

Centers on individual craftsmanship and artistic expression, emphasizing distinctive techniques and creation of works that can be retained long term and enter art and craft markets, rather than time-sensitive customer commissions.

Better suited to people wanting to refine their craft over time in a personal style and create independently; those less interested in immediate customer needs and the retail pace may choose this direction.
Outputs are lasting craft works: concept and prototyping, creation through materials and techniques, completion and signing, display and sales.
Craft Artists

Centers on fine art creation and exhibition, emphasizing artistic concepts, series of works, and exhibitions, with evaluation in art and academic fields and delivery cycles based on creation and exhibition plans.
Better suited to people aspiring to artistic expression and sustained creation; those less interested in service work requiring rapid delivery within budgets and bookings may choose this direction.
Outputs are artworks and exhibitions: concepts and sketches, creation and production, curation and exhibition, criticism and sales.
Fine Artists (Including Painters, Sculptors, and Illustrators)

Centers on displays of durable goods and props and window visuals, emphasizing visual merchandising and product presentation. Materials and props are reusable and do not involve flower preservation or conditioning.
Better suited to people who prefer retail visuals and merchandise displays and do not want to handle losses and preservation of living materials.
Outputs are display and window plans: themes and colors, combinations of props and products, setup and maintenance, and records of results.
Merchandise Displayers and Window Trimmers

Centers on overall exhibition and scene design, structures, and construction, involving engineering, lighting, and safety, with larger project scale and authority. Flowers are only one possible element.

Better suited to people able to handle project-based design, coordination among parties, and structural and safety requirements; those wanting only to shape floral materials are better suited to this occupation.
Outputs are overall exhibition and scene plans: concepts and drawings, materials and structures, construction and installation, dismantling and recycling.
Set and Exhibit Designers

Centers on product sales and customer service, emphasizing product knowledge, closing sales, and after-sales service. Work concerns shelves and orders rather than floral selection, conditioning, and shaping.

Better suited to people who prefer sales and service and derive their main satisfaction from closing sales and customer relationships; those wanting to make pieces by hand are better suited to this occupation.
Outputs are sales and service results: reception and recommendations, ordering and payment, stock and display maintenance, after-sales service and repeat purchases.
Retail Salespersons

Transition | This page places adjacent occupations side by side by object, delivery, and retention period to help you decide which type of work you want to pursue long term. Whichever direction you choose, readiness for work depends on understanding materials and customer needs, delivering within budgets and schedules, and passing a practical assessment recognized by an employer or mentor; interest questionnaires only raise questions.

What personality suits this work? This occupation values willingness to work with your hands, aesthetic sensitivity, and patient communication more than a particular personality type. Its O*NET interest code is RAC (Realistic—Artistic—Conventional), which can be an exploration starting point.

An introversion label does not determine employability. Face-to-face communication is 100% daily and telephone communication 95% daily; this does not establish that production is mainly solitary. Observe actual communication responsibilities.

What should I prepare before entry? First understand the actual shop pace (peak-season overtime, prolonged standing, repetitive hand movements, and flower losses) and prepare basic flower care and tool-use knowledge. You can begin as a flower shop assistant or peak-season helper.

Where does daily pressure mainly come from? Fixed delivery deadlines, last-minute order changes, and flower losses. O*NET work context reports time pressure at 86% daily and telephone communication at 95% daily.

Are there physical requirements? Work requires prolonged standing and hand use and may involve frequent movement between refrigerated and room-temperature areas. Pollen and plant sap may cause allergies. Specific employment and medical examination requirements depend on employers and local laws; this page provides no medical examination conclusions.

US O*NET education: 71% high school / 24% below high school / 5% postsecondary certificate; BLS typical education is high school. This does not mean formal education is usually unnecessary. JobZone1—2 is a general preparation description; check Chinese recruitment separately.

Can long-term work harm health? Prolonged standing, repetitive hand movements, and cuts from sharp tools are practical costs. Use protective equipment, take work breaks, protect cuts, and prevent slips in refrigerated and wet areas.

Career progression and transition directions? Progress from shop assistant to floral designer, shop supervisor, and event floral coordinator, or move into flower wholesaling, variety and preservation support, floral teaching, or an independent studio. Moving between directions requires learning materials and settings anew.

entries.answer: Under O*NET-SOC 27-1023.00, this occupation designs, cuts, and arranges fresh, dried, or artificial flowers and foliage for bouquets, wreaths, table arrangements, corsages, flower baskets, and scene decorations. Work includes confirming occasion and budget with customers, selecting and purchasing materials, incoming inspection and cutting and conditioning, color and form production, packaging and pricing, delivery and on-site setup, shop displays and inventory care, and explaining care to customers. It excludes large-scale flower and foliage cultivation and postharvest handling, general shop business management, and large exhibition construction.
entries.question: What exactly does this occupation do?

entries.answer: Craft and fine artists focus on individual creation and lasting works, with evaluation in art and craft fields. Merchandise displayers and window trimmers mainly display durable goods and props without flower preservation. This occupation works with fresh, dried, and artificial flowers, delivering pieces that change over time according to customer requirements and schedules, emphasizing preservation, timeliness, and on-site effect. Material properties, delivery deadlines, and responsibility boundaries differ.
entries.question: How does it differ from craft artists and merchandise displayers?

entries.answer: The 2025 median annual wage was 37,360 dollars (median hourly wage 17.96 dollars); 2025 employment was about 45,200 (BLS Employment Projections base year). Employment is projected to decline about -6% during 2025—2035, with about 5,200 average annual job openings (mainly replacement needs). These use US O*NET / BLS definitions and do not apply to other jurisdictions.

entries.answer: O*NET work context shows daily time pressure 86%, daily telephone communication 95%, continual or almost continual hand use 86%, continuous standing 73%, repetitive motions 55%, and controlled indoor work (91% daily). Protective equipment, breaks, and reasonable scheduling can reduce strain, but prolonged standing, repetitive hand movements, and peak-season intensity remain practical costs.

entries.answer: Effects mainly concern paperwork, records, and inspiration: tools may assist order, inventory, and loss records, trial quotes and quantity calculations, color and display inspiration searches, shop social media drafts, and delivery scheduling. Floral designers and shop supervisors remain responsible for occasion and budget judgments, flower freshness and conditioning, final color and form choices, on-site production, and delivery confirmation. Task exposure does not equal job replacement.

entries.answer: O*NET shows that this occupation typically requires high school or equivalent education (71% of respondents), while 24% consider less than high school sufficient and 5% require a postsecondary certificate, with techniques learned through on-the-job training (Job Zone 1-2, SVP below 6.0). Actual requirements depend on employer hiring conditions and shop needs.

entries.answer: Having training, obtaining a certificate, receiving employer appointment, and having quote and delivery decision authority are four different states. Flower care and tool safety training and hygiene requirements are generally common requirements; industry association certification is voluntary and does not constitute statutory professional licensing. Imported flower quarantine, food safety (such as edible decorations), and large-installation construction have separate requirements. entries.answer: Common failures include skipped incoming inspection and preservation care, improper sharp-tool use and storage, overloaded peak periods combined with last-minute changes, inaccurate quotes and inventory and loss records, customer and event information used beyond scope, and unclear access and finished-piece protection responsibilities for weddings and events. Key controls are procedural inspection and records, and pausing and escalating according to procedures.

entries.answer: Under US definitions, employment is projected to decline about -6% during 2025—2035, with openings mainly from replacement needs. Projections do not equal personal opportunities; actual opportunities depend on local holiday and wedding consumption and shop structures. Adjacent directions include craft art, merchandise display and window trimming, graphic design, interior design, set and exhibit design, retail sales, landscaping, and artistic coordination (requiring learning materials and techniques anew), as well as flower wholesaling and preservation support, floral teaching, and independent studios.
